briefs.title: Bab el-Mandeb: what a sticky war-risk premium means for landed cost
briefs.bluf: Southern Red Sea war-risk cover has repriced to multiples of its pre-blockade level and is unlikely to normalise this winter, even though no merchant ship has been confirmed struck at sea since late August. For importers the premium, not the missiles, is now the binding cost line.
judgements: War-risk quotes for Saudi-linked tonnage have tripled since summer; general transit cover remains far above the 0.2–0.3% of hull value seen for non-exposed ships.
Large container lines are cautiously routing services back through Suez, so physical transit risk and priced risk have decoupled.
A single strike on a non-Saudi container ship would likely reverse the Suez return within days: a low-probability, high-impact tail.
briefs.situation: The Houthis declared a blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July and enforced it with strikes on Saudi tankers through 24 August. Since then the sea lane has been quiet while missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory continued in late September. Insurers have not followed the quiet: Reuters reported on 24 September that the cost of insuring a tanker loaded at Yanbu had tripled in weeks, and market commentary puts southern Red Sea additional premiums around 3% of hull value for exposed risks. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have nonetheless moved several Gemini services back to Suez.

readings.note: Corridor posture elevated; Suez return partial
War-risk proxy sticky at elevated level
Crude routing via Red Sea under cost pressure

scenarios.name: Sticky premium
scenarios.text: No new strikes at sea; premiums ease slowly but stay well above pre-July levels into Q1 2027.

scenarios.name: Re-escalation
scenarios.text: Strikes on Saudi-linked tankers resume once Yanbu loadings pick up; carriers pause Suez returns and freight reprices.

scenarios.name: De-escalation
scenarios.text: Regional talks produce a credible pause; premiums fall back toward 1% of hull value or lower.

briefs.title: Grain corridor stress and the bread-price lag
briefs.bluf: The Black Sea has become a two-way port war that has choked both Ukrainian and Russian grain exports. Wheat futures are up about a fifth year on year; the household bread-price effect arrives with a lag of one to two quarters, hitting import-dependent MENA, African and South Asian buyers first.
judgements: Ukraine's seaborne grain exports fell to 0.81 Mt in September from 2.1 Mt a year earlier, despite Danube and Romanian rerouting.
Russia's Black Sea and Azov grain exports collapsed to about 0.3 Mt in September from 4.74 Mt, pushing trials via Murmansk and Baltic terminals.
Strikes near Romanian and Bulgarian waters raise the NATO-flank dimension and the insurance cost of every remaining corridor.
briefs.situation: Ambrey Analytics counts 317 merchant and other vessels hit in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, more than four times the prior half-year. Ukraine suspended operations at its Black Sea ports in late July; a container ship was sunk by naval drones off Bulgaria on 28 October. On 10 November India signalled readiness to help broker food corridors, but any deal would need Türkiye's Bosphorus role, insurers and an inspection mechanism like the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative.

readings.note: Export capacity and price pressure both elevated
Food channel adding to composite stress

scenarios.name: Grinding constraint
scenarios.text: Attacks continue at current tempo; exports stay near half of normal via rail and Danube; prices drift higher into spring.

scenarios.name: Corridor deal
scenarios.text: A brokered food corridor reopens some Odesa capacity; futures retrace part of the year's gain.

scenarios.name: Wider escalation
scenarios.text: Strikes in NATO members' territorial waters trigger escorts or new restrictions; freight and insurance spike.

briefs.title: Chips, copper and a strait: reading tension through the supply chain
briefs.bluf: A possible unannounced PLA exercise simulating Taiwan's isolation puts the strait back into supply-chain pricing. The first-order transmission is marine insurance and freight in the western Pacific, not chip prices; a sustained disruption would show up in autos, industrial electronics and medical devices months later.
judgements: More than 100 PLA Navy and China Coast Guard vessels were reported operating in the West Pacific on 3 November, in two concentrations between Taiwan and its partners.
Air activity is uneven: October sorties were lower than a year earlier, but joint combat readiness patrols hit a 2026 high of five.
Rare-earth leverage is the slower channel: TSMC is reportedly seeking alternatives to rare-earth magnets for factory automation.
briefs.situation: AEI and ISW assessed on 6 November that the PRC may be running a major unannounced exercise that simulates surrounding and isolating Taiwan, potentially larger than 'Justice Mission 2025' and drawing on three theater commands, including the Liaoning carrier group, with the Fujian carrier seen leaving Sanya on 2 November. Taiwan Security Monitor counted 232 PLA sorties in October and 12 PRC government-vessel incursions, tying the year's high. Taiwan's ITRI plans a rare-earth facility to cover half of domestic demand by 2030.

readings.note: Naval posture elevated; air tempo mixed
Theater stress spills into regional risk
Copper and chip-input pressure modest so far

scenarios.text: Deployments return to port within weeks; insurance and freight retrace; no chip shipment disruption.

scenarios.name: Prolonged grey-zone pressure
scenarios.text: Coast Guard 'law-enforcement patrols' and inspections become routine east of Taiwan; premiums stay elevated.

scenarios.name: Quarantine-style disruption
scenarios.text: Shipments are delayed or inspected; downstream shortages build over three to six months.

briefs.title: GNSS jamming and undersea cables: the infrastructure flank
briefs.bluf: In the Baltic, the two infrastructure threats are diverging: NATO reports a drastic drop in undersea-infrastructure incidents since Baltic Sentry began, while satellite-navigation interference has intensified through 2026. The live risk to shipping and aviation is now in the spectrum, not on the seabed.
judgements: NATO told the European Parliament on 3 November that its last observed Baltic undersea-infrastructure incident was in January 2026 and limited in impact.
Poland's National Institute of Telecommunications recorded all-band GNSS interference on 70% of days in May and June around the Tri-City area.
Deterrence is hard to prove: the threat may have moved to other regions or domains rather than disappeared.
briefs.situation: Baltic Sentry, launched on 14 January 2025, combines frigates, maritime patrol aircraft and naval drones with the MAINSAIL data tool. Separately, the Commission funded two regional cable-security hubs (€5.8m) and a €40m repair-capacity call in June 2026. On the spectrum side, Finland's Traficom reports increased disruption in the eastern Gulf of Finland, and NATO tested its GANDALF 4 jamming-detection sensor at sea in July. Researchers have traced Baltic interference to electronic-warfare sites in Kaliningrad.

readings.note: Spectrum stress up, cable incidents down

scenarios.name: Persistent spectrum pressure
scenarios.text: Jamming continues at 2026 levels; cable incidents stay rare; costs fall on aviation and shipping navigation.

scenarios.name: Seabed relapse
scenarios.text: A new cable or pipeline incident tests attribution and shadow-fleet sanctions enforcement.

scenarios.name: Easing
scenarios.text: Interference subsides after diplomatic or technical countermeasures.
